en: In the Dharma-realm school, the Chapter on the Lotus:
The śramaṇa Ciyun from the Clear Qiantang River, Xufa, compiled this together with his disciple Faxian.
Just as the myriad phenomena reach their ultimate limit in emptiness, and the hundred rivers and various streams reach their ultimate limit in the ocean, so it is with all sages and worthies.

It reaches its ultimate consummation in the Buddha; among all teachings, it reaches its ultimate consummation in the perfection of the *Avataṃsaka*. Among the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, the *Avataṃsaka* is the ultimate;

among the commentaries and exegeses of the ancient masters, that of Xianshou is the ultimate. Therefore, I shall now rely upon those teachings and contemplations to open and synthesize the five gates and one hundred dharmas.
Were it not for the Lotus Sūtra, there would be no means by which to employ metaphors for awakening.

At the time of its initial exposition, the sun rose and the flower first blossomed; its reflection appeared upon the high waters, and its color and fragrance began to spread, whereupon people and bees gathered in full assembly.
This is the time when it first appears. At one day’s rise, it opens and closes unpredictably with the wind.

At mealtime (the hour of *chen*), its color becomes somewhat pale, its fragrance gradually fades, and its reflection lowers toward the water; this is called the "first turning. At midday, it appears white from afar and red when viewed closely.

When the reflection falls into the deep water, it is called the "middle turning. If it is at the hour of *bú* (the seventh watch, approximately 3–5 p.m.), the color is somewhat deeper and the fragrance slightly heavier;

the reflection is near the high water. This is called the "later turning," which constitutes the time of the general turning-reflection. Second, when the sun has set and the flowers are about to close, the reflection returns to the high water;
the color and fragrance are as they were at first, and humans and bees gather once more. This is the time of returning reflection. Third.

The distinct periods are as described above. What of the universal period? Within a single moment, color, fragrance, light, and shadow are fully present without exception, no different from any other;
this is called "a single thought-moment. A single fragrance, scent, color, or light pervades all three times, responding to the mind according to its measure;
this is called "the completion of a single transformation. Second, since the opening and closing of the three periods of the day is thus, so too was it for the preceding [yesterday].
In subsequent days (that is, the future), the three periods [of the day] are likewise so; this is called "pervading the three intervals" (3).

The initial illumination and subsequent reflection of the fragrant light on a previous day are identical to the initial illumination and subsequent reflection on today and tomorrow; this is called "encompassing similar eons" (4).

The intermediate transformation of fragrance, shadow, light, and color on a subsequent day is identical to the initial and final transformations on a previous day and today; this is called "gathering different eons" (5). One.

One contemplates flowers and fruits; they do not differ from those of past and future days, months, years, and seasons. Nor do the flowers and fruits of past and future days, months, years, and seasons differ from what is contemplated now.
This is called "contemplation encompassing kalpas. (6) Within the single thought-moment that encompasses these past and future times, there are further many thought-moments.
(7) Within those many thoughts, further many periods of time are subsumed; this is called "further repeated inclusion. (8) As it is with this pond, so it is with that pond;
as it is in the eastern lands, so it is in the Western Regions; this is called "different realms and times.

(9) All the kalpas and thoughts of both these and those, whether east or west, mutually include one another in infinite layers; this is called "mutual inclusion. (10) It is the thought itself that is the kalpa; it is not...
Thought is not an eon (*kalpa*), for time has no substantial body; it is established based upon the flower. Since the flower is already pervasive and interfused, time is likewise unimpeded.
This is called "the fundamental subsuming the derivative" (10).

Next, the ritual procedure is set forth. Taking the original planting of flowers as the root and the transplanting and dividing of flowers as the branches constitutes the distinction between root and branch;

while their names and forms are identical in essence, they differ according to superior, middling, and inferior grades. This is termed the "distinction between root and branch. Furthermore, when many flowers bloom from a single original seed, this is termed "arising of branches based upon the root."

(2) Although there are many branches and lineages, they do not depart from the original seed; this is called "subsuming the derivative and returning to the fundamental. (3) Without the fundamental seed, there would be no way for the retinue to arise in succession;
without the retinue, there would be no way to manifest the fundamental original seed; this is called "the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative."

(4) The lotus opens in nine grades, its colors divided into four types; these manifest according to karma—how could they have a fixed location? Thus they are called "indeterminate according to capacity.
(5) Those who see and hear one another are called "manifest," while those who do not see or hear one another are called "secret.

Being on the same flower yet constituting both manifest and secret is called "simultaneity of manifest and secret. (6) The petals, filaments, ovary, and fruit are simultaneously complete; this is called...
(7) At one time, it is expounded all at once. (8) Softly nourishing and tranquilly sustaining, it benefits human "bees" and is named "Silent Quiescence.

When the lotus has fully matured, it falls into the mud and is born again; thus revolving in succession, it is never severed throughout the three periods of time, and is therefore named "Pervading the Three Intervals."
(9) From a single lotus flower, immeasurable lotus flowers are produced; from one pond of flowers, countless ponds of flowers are divided forth.
This is called the "inexhaustible layering" (10).

Third, the classification according to teaching (*yàojiào*): 1. To say that the flower arises from the conditions of branches, stems, water, and soil, and to practice the contemplation of arising and ceasing (*shēngmiè guān*), is called the Small Teaching (*xiǎojiào*).

2. To recognize that the lotus arises from the lotus root (*liánǎo*) and to practice the contemplation of the absence of self-nature (*wúxìng guān*), is called the Initial Teaching (*shǐjiào*). 3. To know that the flower arises from within the lotus seed (*liánshí*) and to practice the contemplation of dependent origination (*yuánqǐ guān*), is called the Final Teaching (*zhōngjiào*).

4. To realize that the flower arises from the rolled-up filaments (*héxīn*) within the lotus ovary (*liánrou*), [and to practice the contemplation of the non-arising of all phenomena], is called the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).

4. One who practices the contemplation of the ultimate reality is called a follower of the Sudden Teaching (*don-gyü*). (4) When awakening to the growth of a lotus flower, one sees that the lotus seed, root, and stem, as well as the conditions of water and soil, are all fully present.

One who practices the contemplation of perfect interpenetration is called a follower of the Perfect Teaching (*dön-gyü*). (5) If we employ metaphors for the phenomena (*chos-sa*) explained by these teachings:
first, within the Lesser Vehicle (*sō-kyō*), the "skin" metaphorizes the suffering within the realms (*kai-nai ku*), and the "flesh" metaphorizes [the aggregates] within the realms.

The mud symbolizes the accumulation (*upādāna*) outside the realms; the water symbolizes the suffering (*duḥkha*) outside the realms. The sprout piercing and breaking through the skin symbolizes the cessation (*nirodha*) within the realms;

the sprout piercing and breaking through the flesh symbolizes the path (*mārga*) within the realms. The sprout emerging above the mud symbolizes the path outside the realms; the sprout emerging from the water symbolizes the cessation outside the realms.
The single layer of skin, flesh, mud, and grass covering it from above symbolizes the condition of ignorance (*avidyā-pratyaya*), which possesses the power to produce [existence].

This illustrates the conditions for action (*karma-pratyaya*). Containing within it a lotus bud with its flowers and fruits fully prepared, it illustrates consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).

Its internal moisture illustrates craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*). Its being perfectly round and coiled so that it cannot emerge illustrates birth, old age, and death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*). The sprout’s tip is already stirring.
The piercing of the skin and flesh symbolizes the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*). That they no longer grow back within the skin and flesh symbolizes the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

The roots, stems, flowers, and fruits emerging from outside the skin and mud symbolize the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).

The moistening dew and rain symbolize the cessation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*). Emerging above the surface of the water and opening and closing as they please symbolizes the cessation of birth, old age, and death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*). (3) Next, the beginning...

In the Teaching (Dharma), the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇavāda) holds that the lotus is substantially existent; this is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva). To realize that the dependent [nature] exists only as a provisional designation is the nature of dependence on others (paratantra-svabhāva).
Before the lotus seed has encountered conditions, and after the petals have fallen and the flower has dropped, there are fundamentally no signs of the arising or ceasing of flowers or fruits;
this is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva). (3) In the School of Emptiness (Śūnyatāvāda), the leaves flutter and scatter with the wind and rain, and the flowers follow...

Bees and butterflies gather and alight; this is the emptiness of the self (*ātma-śūnyatā*). The lotus stalks and buds are all empty and without substance; this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Being hollow within and solid without, it is free from both existence and non-existence; this is true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*). (4) Third, the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*): the lotus seed is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-stha-gotra*).

(5) Descending into the muddy pool and emerging from the mire represents the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), which is called "enlightenment by name" (*nāma-vijñapti-bodhi*). Abiding in emptiness while about to unfurl its petals represents the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*); its filaments...

The calyx can be identified. When the ten petals open toward the sun and turn back, this is called "similar awakening" (*sadr̥śa-bodha*); they unfold and achieve maturity, bearing bees and butterflies—this is the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

When the filaments and leaves are about to fall and the lotus seed-vessel remains alone, it is called "partial awakening" (*yathābhāga-bodha*); these are all instances of initial awakening (*ādi-bodha*).
(6) When the flower petals have completely withered and only the calyx remains, it is ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodha*). (7) These are the four sudden teachings (*catasraḥ kṣipra-dharmāḥ*).
Within the lotus seed is the nature of dependent origination; this is self-awakened wisdom. Within the lotus seed is the unchanging nature;
this is the object of self-awakening. (8) Fifth, the Perfect Teaching: the lotus pod, root, and stem are the phenomenal dharma-realm. (9) The hollow space within is the noumenal dharma-realm.
(2) That which is empty within yet exists without, being as one without obstruction, is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomenon and noumenon. (3)

The lotus root, leaves, filaments, and stamens all appear simultaneously and pervasively; this is the dharma-realm of non-obstruction in all things. (4) The roots, fruit, flowers, and leaves benefit humans and bees;

this is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). (1) Its fragrance spreads everywhere without any defilement; this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). (2) Though born from a muddy pool, it is not disgraced;
this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). (3) It only increases and never declines; this is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). (4)
(5) Abiding in tranquility and cultivating non-action to achieve pliancy is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā). (6) The flowers bloom when the sun rises and close when the sun sets;

this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā). (7) Following the conditions of wind and water, rising in the east and falling in the west, surging in the south and subsiding in the north—this is the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).

(8) For the sake of the lotus, the stalk supports the flower and the leaves form a canopy, while the filaments surround the ovary; this is the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā). Whether it be the root or the seed—
All possess the functional capacity to produce [their effects]; this is the power of *bala* (9). Immeasurable colored lights mutually reflect one another with brilliant radiance;
this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) (10).

Fourth, the Manifestation of the Doctrine (*siddhānta-nirdeśa*): 1. I possess innumerable varieties of colored lotuses; this is called "the existence of both self and phenomena" (*ātma-dharma-sad-bhāva*). 2. These innumerable lotuses are not possessed by me alone;
this is called "the existence of phenomena and the non-existence of self" (*dharma-sat-ātma-asad-bhāva*). 3. Only the present is perceived, while the past and future are unknown;

this is called "the non-existence of phenomena in the past and future" (*dharmasya-atītānāgata-asad-bhāva*). 4. The essence and characteristics are real, whereas the reflection is false; this is called "manifesting the provisional and the real" (*pratyakṣa-prajñapti-tattva*). 5. The Flower.
The essence and characteristics are provisional; the essence and characteristics of the seed are real. This is called the conventional, the false, the true, and the real.

(5) Flowers and fruits all belong to the category of having names but no substance; they are merely names for all phenomena. (6) These six gates above are all metaphors for the Hīnayāna school that adheres to the dharma-attachment of following appearances.

As for the flowers and fruits, they both arise from the lotus root; these appearances are not non-existent, and this is called the Yogācāra-dharmalakṣaṇa (Consciousness-only with Characteristics). (7)

(8) These roots and stems, though possessing external forms, lack any internal substance; this is called "true emptiness and signlessness. (9) The lotus flower arises from the dharma of the lotus seed which depends on others;
the lotus seed follows various conditions and arises without obstruction; this is called "the dependent origination of the storehouse-consciousness.
(10) The lotus seed unfolds from within the rolled-up lotus bud; the nature of the rolled-up lotus bud is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; this is called...

The true nature is quiescent. (10) The mind-nature of the rolled-up lotus is fundamentally one true reality; it is free from arising and free from ceasing—this is the ultimate principle of the *dharmadhātu*.
As for the mental characteristics of the rolled-up lotus, its roots, stems, flowers, and fruits are each fully present;

this is the *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination. Both the nature and the characteristics are capable of pervading all; even the currently manifesting roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits are likewise capable of pervading all. This is the Lord.
Layer upon layer, it is called the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm (11).
Fifth is the contemplation of emptiness: before flowers and fruits have arisen, and after they have already perished, their characteristics are utterly non-existent;

even in the present moment, every thought-instant shifts and passes away, being empty and devoid of intrinsic nature. This is called "True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics" (1). Although they lack such a nature, it does not hinder...
(1) It possesses characteristics; it is neither empty nor existent, yet it is empty and existent. This is called the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*).
(2) Roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all termed the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As they are subsumed within the Dharma-realm, they are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.

Roots and so forth are likewise all subsumed within it without end. This is called universal inclusion and containment (*zhou-bian han-rong*). (3) A lotus seed in a muddy pond sprouts and pierces through flesh; this is called hell.
The Dharma-realm. (1) Seeing with aversion (*dveṣa*) is like a black lotus; emerging from the skin, it is called the dharma-realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
(2) Seeing with greed (*lobha*) is like a green lotus; penetrating the mud, it is called the dharma-realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). (3) Seeing with delusion (*moha*) is like a blue lotus;

level with the mud, it is called the dharma-realm of asuras. (4) Seeing with pride (*māna*) is like a yellow lotus; emerging from the mud and remaining in the water, it is called the dharma-realm of humans. [This concerns] precepts.
Knowledge and vision like a white lotus (5), growing within the water, is called the Dharma-realm of the devas.

Knowledge and vision like a red lotus (6), level with the surface of the water, is called the Dharma-realm of the śrāvakas. Knowledge and vision like a purple lotus (7), emerging above the water, is called the Dharma-realm of the pratyekabuddhas.
Knowledge and vision like a crimson lotus (8), situated in the air, is called the Dharma-realm of the bodhisattvas.
(9) To transcend knowledge and vision is like the blue lotus. "Just emerging from the pond" refers to the initial stage (*ādi*).

When it first reaches the surface of the pond, it is the final stage (*anta*). When it suddenly pierces through the top of the pond, it is the sudden stage (*tun*). Emerging directly above the pond, about to unfold in full bloom, is the perfect stage (*yuan*).

Turning toward the sun to open is called the Dharma-realm of the Buddha. To awaken to knowledge and vision is like the golden lotus. (10) The initial opening of the flower's stamen represents the Small Teaching (*hīnayāna*). The flower floating [upon the water]... [represents the Great Teaching].

The Lotus Manifests. In the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō), it closes with the downward wind; in the Empty Teaching (Kūkyō), it opens with the upward wind; in the Phenomenal Teaching (Sōkyō), the flowers close as the sun sets;

in the Sudden Teaching (Tongyō)—because it is the penetration of the essence (shūtsū)—the flowers open as the sun rises; in the Final Teaching (Shūkyō)—because it is the penetration of the doctrine (setsutsū)—it opens upon the celestial sun, bringing joy to devas and humans, which is the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ichijō).
In contrast, when it opens beneath the water of the pond, fish and shrimp receive its shade; this is the meaning of the Two Vehicles (Nishō). It does not rise above.

It does not sink; it opens facing the wind. Birds come and go; bees and butterflies gather and play. This is the meaning of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). The above constitutes the correspondence between names and teachings (*nāmavyavahāra*) and their meanings (*artha*).
(1) The lotus stalk, stamens, ovary, and fruit are the phenomena (*dharma*). The stamens are empty on the outside; the ovary and fruit are empty within. This is the principle (*tattva*).

This is collectively termed the correspondence between phenomena and principle (*dharmatattva*). (2) The nature of the lotus seed is without arising or ceasing. This is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). [The text ends with: "Revolving..."

The lotus mind turning according to conditions is wisdom (*jñāna*). This constitutes the correspondence between object and wisdom. (3) The sprout, root, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit all possess the power of growth;
this is practice (*caryā*). The five successive stages—planting the seed, germination, growth, maturation, and shedding—are the levels (*avasthā*).
(4) This is the correspondence of practice and position. (5) The lotus flower is the cause; the lotus seed is the fruit. This is the correspondence of cause and effect. (6) The lotus pod.
The lotus seed is the primary; the lotus husk is the secondary. The lotus kernel is the primary; the lotus pond is the secondary. The lotus flower is the primary.
This is the "Correct" (zhèng). It corresponds to the "Support and Supported" (yīzhèng duì). (6) Both take the four subtle elements and eight dharmas as their substance; this is the "Essence" (tǐ).

Yet they possess the functional capacities for growth, development, opening, expansion, and branching; this is the "Function" (yòng). This corresponds to the "Essence and Function" (tǐyòng duì). (7) They can open and close according to the sun; they can bow and lift according to the wind;

they can support raindrops that turn like pearls; and they can cover ponds to manifest reflections—all of which are human qualities. That which they possess—the white lotus and the green... [text ends]

The branches, red blossoms bordering the leaves, yellow stamens and purple petals, pale flesh and dark skin—all these are phenomena (*dharma*). This constitutes the correspondence of person and phenomenon (8).
Beautiful reflections of flowers, beautiful pearls, beautiful lotus seeds, and beautiful lotus roots—all these are favorable (*anuloma*).

Unbeautiful reflections of flowers, unbeautiful pearls, unbeautiful lotus seeds, and unbeautiful lotus roots—all these are unfavorable (*pratiloma*). This is called the correspondence of the favorable and the unfavorable (9). [The category of] beautiful and unbeautiful flowers.
"Leaves, lotus roots, fruits, pearls, and reflections—these are the 'responses' (*ying*). Whether it be favorable or unfavorable wind, sun, rain, water, or mud—these are the 'conditions' (*gan*).
It is like withered flowers following the scorching sun, their shadows falling upon turbid water; yellow leaves tossed by a wild wind, or pearls scattered by a torrential rain;

lotus roots shifted to a barren pool, or tiny seeds fallen into coarse mud. This is the response to adverse conditions. It is like fresh flowers following the bright sun, their shadows falling upon clear water.

Green leaves follow the gentle breeze; pearls scatter upon the sweet rain. Fertile lotus roots are transplanted to rich ponds; great seeds fall into beautiful mud. This is called "Responsive Resonance" (*ganying*); it is named the "Gate of Responsive Resonance.

(10) The filaments are the cause and the lotus pedestal is the fruit; they are fully present at the same time. This is called the "Gate of Simultaneous Fulfillment and Correspondence" (*dongsong juzu xiangying men*).
(1) The anthers are narrow while the flower is broad; the flower is broad while the fruit is narrow; the petals are broad while the filaments are narrow; the ovary—

The broad contains the narrow; there is no obstruction and all is sovereign. This is called the Gate of Unobstructed Sovereignty over the Broad and the Narrow. (2) The lotus pedestal is one, yet the filaments and petals are many;

the flower petal is one, yet the lotus filaments are many; the seed pod is one, yet the seeds within are many. This is called the Gate of the Mutual Interpenetration of One and Many Without Confusion.
(3) The pedestal is within, the filaments are in the center, and the petals encircle the outside. If one speaks of the "lotus flower," then the pedestal and the filaments are themselves the petals.

If one speaks of the lotus pod (*kośa*), then the filaments and petals are the pedestal (*maṇḍala*). This is called the Gate of the Mutual Identity of All Dharmas (4). When it is the stamen (*keśara*), the [other parts] are hidden; when it is the flower (*puṣpa*), they are manifest.

When the leaves and petals are manifest, the filaments and pedestal are hidden. When the lotus pod is manifest, the lotus seeds (*bīja*) are hidden. When it opens, they are manifest; when it closes, they are hidden.
When it blooms, they are manifest; when it withers, they are hidden. This is called the Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of the Secret and the Manifest (5). One seed carries many.
Each son enters one chamber; each son likewise does so. One platform, accompanied by many sons, enters many filaments.
One filament, accompanied by one chamber and many filaments, enters one petal. Each filament likewise does so. One petal, accompanied by many filament-petals, enters one lotus platform.
Each leaf is likewise so. Within each calyx, there are many stamens and petals that enter into many seeds;

this is true for every calyx. Viewed in this manner, they are layered upon one another without end; this is called the "Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net. (6) Within the flowers, the stamens are contained within the pistils.
Within the calyx are many seeds; within the seeds are present all roots, stems, flowers, and fruits. This is called the "Gate of Subtle Mutual Containment and Establishment.
(7) To see one leaf, one filament, or one seed is to see many leaves, many filaments, and many seeds. To see one flower is to see the filaments and the calyx.
To see the empty ovary is to see the emptiness of the seeds. This is called "Manifesting the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena."

The Gate of Arising Understanding (8). From the formation of the calyx to the ripening of the fruit, there is growth day and night, accumulated over months and years; though many temporal stages intervene, they do not depart from the present moment.

This is called the Gate of the Ten Ages Being Separated Yet Simultaneously Accomplished (9). The lotus flower is the cause and the lotus seed is the fruit; these constitute three propositions. First, regarding the primary cause and the accompanying causes:
whichever single part, such as the flower or leaf, is taken as the primary, the remaining many parts, such as the filaments and leaves, serve as the accompaniments.

(9) The Gate of the Perfectly Illuminated Endowment with Principal and Retinue (*pradhāna-parivāra-saṃpūrṇa-vidyotana-guṇavat-mukha*). There are three aspects of principal and retinue: first, the fruit as principal and its retinue; one seed-pod is the principal, while the many remaining pods are the retinue. Second, the fruit as principal and its retinue;

one lotus pod is the principal, while the many remaining petals are the retinue. Third, the cause as principal and its retinue; one lotus pod is the principal, while the many remaining petals are the retinue. Viewed from one another, these principals and retinues are layered upon one another;

thus it is named the Gate of the Perfectly Illuminated Endowment with Principal and Retinue. (10) The lotus is endowed with leaves, stamens, a receptacle, and seeds; this is named... [the Gate of the Perfectly Illuminated Endowment with All Qualities].

1. The general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): The single stamen, pericarp, and seed-vessel are not themselves the flower; this is called the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). 2. The stamen, petals, and pericarp, etc., together constitute a single flower;

this is called the common characteristic (*sabhāga-lakṣaṇa*). 3. The lotus pericarp is not the same as the stamens, petals, and so forth; this is called the distinct characteristic (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*). 4. A single flower is formed by gathering the conditions of the various stamens, petals, pericarps, and so forth;

this is called the characteristic of formation (*niṣpatti-lakṣaṇa*). 5. The stamens, petals, pericarps, and so forth, each abide in their own respective positions; this is called... [the characteristic of abiding].

The aspect of disintegration. (6) Just as it is with one flower, so it is with ten mysteries and six aspects; if one considers many flowers, as well as other roots, stems, leaves, and so forth, the ten mysteries and six aspects are likewise the same.
The lotus serves as an analogy for this; other metaphors may be understood by extension.

In every dharma and at every moment, in every particle of dust and in every teaching and contemplation, one may say that the vehicle of the Dharma is spread before the six sense faculties, and its sound and light are distributed throughout the realm of myriad transformations. Those who read this later should examine it with repeated care.

(Ten times, ten modes, ten realms, ten pairs, ten mysteries, and ten perfections make sixty. Together with the four dharma-realms and the six aspects, they total seventy. Three times, three awakenings, three contemplations, and eleven schools make ninety.

Each of the five teachings is further divided into five—namely, the Four Truths, Dependent Origination, the Three Natures, the Three Emptinesses, and the two types of self-awakening—which together constitute the five [subdivisions], thus forming one hundred dharma-gates. If one further expands the three stages of initial awakening within the three awakenings, along with the five gates of the Truths, Dependent Origination, Nature, Emptiness, and Awakening, all of these are opened up, resulting in one hundred and twenty layers of dharmas and metaphors.)
